raw_case_text:
A 44-year-old woman with an 18-year history of ASS and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) overlap complicated by 5 years of nonspecific interstitial pneumonitis (NSIP) presented to the emergency department with 2 weeks of progressively worsening dyspnea and cough. The patient was diagnosed with polymyositis via muscle biopsy approximately 20 years prior. At 38 years of age, she developed progressively worsening exertional dyspnea. Anti-Jo-1 antibodies were positive, confirming a diagnosis of ASS. Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed bilateral subpleural ground glass reticulation and fibrosis, consistent with NSIP. A transbronchial lung biopsy also confirmed NSIP. Current immunosuppressive regimen included tacrolimus and hydroxychloroquine for ASS.
Initial blood pressure was 149/59 mm Hg, heart rate of 103/minute, respiratory rate of 26/minute, temperature 38.2 C, and pulse oximetry (SpO2) 79% on room air. The patient appeared to be in mild to moderate respiratory distress and had coarse bi-basilar crackles. Admission chest radiography showed new diffuse bilateral patchy alveolar and interstitial opacities (Figure 1). Initial laboratory data showed a white blood cell count of 24 500/mm3 (38% neutrophils and 54% lymphocytes), a hemoglobin of 12.2 g/dL, platelet count of 268 000, blood urea nitrogen 26, creatinine 1.01 mg/dL, and potassium 5.0 mEq/L. Initial differential diagnoses included the adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) from infection versus an acute exacerbation of ILD.
She was admitted to the intensive care unit and initially supported with high-flow oxygen via nasal cannula. Empiric antimicrobials targeting health care-associated pathogens and influenza were started for a working diagnosis of infectious pneumonia-induced ARDS in an immunocompromised host.
Urine Streptococcus, Legionella, Histoplasma, and Blastomycosis antigens were negative. Sputum gram stain and culture, sputum fungal culture, respiratory influenza nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT), respiratory viral NAAT, serum cytomegalovirus NAAT, Pneumocystis jiroveci direct fluorescent antibody, and serum Aspergillus galactomannan antigen were all negative.
On hospital day 2, chest CT revealed bilateral patchy consolidation and multiple enlarged axillary and mediastinal lymph nodes (Figure 2). On hospital day 3, her hypoxemia and clinical condition continued to decline necessitating endotracheal intubation. Bronchoscopy for airway examination was unremarkable. Bronchoalveolar lavage for infectious testing was also negative. On hospital day 5, video-assisted thoracoscopic biopsies were taken from the right middle and lower lobes. Histopathology revealed peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (PTCL-NOS; Figure 3A and B). Staging workup revealed stage 4 disease. On hospital day 10, a chemotherapeutic regimen of cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone was started. Chest CT revealed interval improvement in pulmonary infiltrates and patchy consolidation (Figure 4), and the patient was extubated on hospital day 13 and discharged home on hospital day 28 with 3 liters per minute oxygen.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 44-year-old woman with an 18-year history of antisynthetase syndrome and rheumatoid arthritis overlap complicated by nonspecific interstitial pneumonia presented with a 2-week history of progressively worsening dyspnea and cough.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with biopsy-proven polymyositis ~20 years earlier, anti-Jo-1-positive antisynthetase syndrome (ASS) and rheumatoid arthritis overlap 18 years earlier, and transbronchial biopsy-proven nonspecific interstitial pneumonitis (NSIP) at age 38 (5 years prior), the patient was maintained on tacrolimus and hydroxychloroquine. She presented to the emergency department after 2 weeks of progressively worsening shortness of breath and cough.
subjective.past_medical_history: Polymyositis (diagnosed 20 years prior); anti-Jo-1-positive antisynthetase syndrome (ASS) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) overlap (18 years); biopsy-proven nonspecific interstitial pneumonitis (NSIP, 5 years).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for progressively worsening dyspnea, cough, and fever. Home medications were tacrolimus and hydroxychloroquine.

objective.physical_examination: Initial vital signs: Blood pressure 149/59 mmHg, heart rate 103 beats/min, respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, temperature 38.2 °C, and SpO2 79% on room air. Physical exam: Mild-to-moderate respiratory distress with coarse bibasilar crackles on lung auscultation.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Leukocytosis with WBC 24,500/mm3 (38% neutrophils, 54% lymphocytes), hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, platelets 268,000/mm3, BUN 26 mg/dL, creatinine 1.01 mg/dL, and potassium 5.0 mEq/L. Negative microbiological workup: Negative urinary Streptococcus pneumoniae, Legionella, Histoplasma, and Blastomyces antigens; negative sputum Gram stain, bacterial/fungal cultures, respiratory viral and influenza NAATs, serum CMV NAAT, Pneumocystis jirovecii direct fluorescent antibody (DFA), and serum Aspergillus galactomannan antigen. Admission chest radiograph: New diffuse bilateral patchy alveolar and interstitial opacities.
objective.advanced_workup: Hospital day 2 chest CT: Bilateral patchy consolidations and multiple enlarged axillary and mediastinal lymph nodes superimposed on chronic subpleural ground-glass reticulation/fibrosis. Hospital day 3 bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Unremarkable airway inspection and negative BAL infectious studies. Hospital day 5 video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) lung biopsies of the right middle and lower lobes: Histopathology and staging workup established stage IV peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (PTCL-NOS).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Stage IV pulmonary peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (PTCL-NOS; confirmed by VATS right middle and lower lobe lung biopsies) masquerading as acute ARDS or interstitial lung disease exacerbation in a patient with antisynthetase syndrome/RA overlap on tacrolimus and hydroxychloroquine, with Pneumocystis jirovecii and other opportunistic infections excluded by negative DFA, BAL, and cultures. Plan and clinical course: Supported initially with high-flow nasal cannula oxygen and empiric broad-spectrum antimicrobials, then intubated on hospital day 3 for progressive hypoxemic respiratory failure. Following VATS confirmation of PTCL-NOS, CHOP chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone) was initiated on hospital day 10, leading to rapid improvement of pulmonary consolidations on repeat chest CT, extubation on hospital day 13, and discharge home on hospital day 28 on 3 L/min supplemental oxygen.
